core.text: Every clause that needs the subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do) after a past main verb uses **the imperfect subjunctive (the past-time 'might / would' form: veniret; built on the infinitive)**. Making it is the easiest job in Latin: take the infinitive (the 'to' form), *venīre* (to come), and add the personal endings — *venīre-m, venīrē-s, venīre-t, venīrē-mus, venīrē-tis, venīre-nt*; passive *-r, -ris, -tur, -mur, -minī, -ntur*. Latin name: *coniūnctīvus imperfectī*.
English has no separate form; *might* or *would* does the job: he came *so that he might see*; she asked *that they would stay*.
Infinitive + personal endings, for every verb, irregular ones included: esse → esset, posse → posset, velle → vellet, ferre → ferret, īre → īret.

invented.la: Māter fīliō imperāvit ut domī manēret.
invented.en: The mother ordered her son to stay at home.
Julius saw to it that the slaves were held.

core.text: *venīret* (imperfect) and *vēnisset* (pluperfect) both sit in the past. The imperfect is built on the present infinitive (*venīre*) and means 'was coming / might come'; the pluperfect on the perfect infinitive (*vēnisse*, to have come) and means 'had come'. Look for -re- against -isse- inside the word.

more.text: Also easy to confuse: the infinitive itself. The whole infinitive is still inside the form — *tacēre* = to be silent, *tacēret* = he might be silent. A word ending in -re is the infinitive; add -m, -s, -t and it is the imperfect subjunctive.

The learner's notes describe the form as 1st stem + -(e)re- + ending, and note that in practice it always looks like the present active infinitive with an ending — even for a deponent verb (passive-looking endings, active meaning: loquitur = he speaks), which has no active infinitive: *lābī* (to slip) → *lāberētur*. Irregular verbs double their consonant in the infinitive and the imperfect subjunctive follows: *es-se → esset, pos-se → posset, vel-le → vellet, fer-re → ferret, māl-le → māllet, nōl-le → nōllet*.

Ørberg's chapter 28 gives the full tables: active *-rem, -rēs, -ret, -rēmus, -rētis, -rent*; passive *-rer, -rēris, -rētur, -rēmur, -rēminī, -rentur*, with *tacēret*, *audīret*, *scrīberet*, *esset* as models. Note the long ē in *-rēs, -rēmus, -rētis, -rēris, -rētur*. Where it is used: purpose, result, indirect command and indirect question after a past verb (Week 6), *cum* clauses (Weeks 6–7), wishes that cannot come true (Week 11), unreal conditions (Week 12).
English has no separate form for it, so 'to be quiet', 'would hear' and 'might come' all end up rendering the same Latin ending.
This is the easiest form in Latin to build. Nothing is cut off the infinitive and no separate stem (what is left of the verb before the ending) has to be found first.
The vowel in front of the ending simply lengthens where Latin's own rules ask it to; the letters you write are still the infinitive followed by the ending.
*vidēret* beside the bare *vidēre*: a person ending has been added, so this is a finite verb (one with a person ending, so it can have a subject), not a 'to' form.

teach.title: Where you meet it

notice.ask: Both stories are in the past. Which word in each sentence has a whole 'to' form (tacēre, venīre) hiding inside it?

teach.say: Once a story moves into the past, every *ut*, *nē* or *cum* clause takes **the imperfect subjunctive (the past-time 'might / would' form: venīret; built on the infinitive)**. *Iūlius imperāvit ut tacēret* — Julius ordered him to be quiet.

check.ask: Which tense of the subjunctive is audīret?

teach.title: Infinitive plus -m, -s, -t
teach.say: Take the present infinitive (the plain 'to' form) whole — *portāre*, *vidēre*, *pōnere*, *venīre* — and add the person endings straight onto the end: **-m** for 'I', **-s** for 'you', **-t** for 'he, she, it'. So *portāre* + *-t* = *portāret*.

check.ask: Write the three singular forms: infinitive plus -m, -s, -t.

teach.title: The plural: -mus, -tis, -nt
teach.say: The plural is made on the same infinitive with the same ordinary endings: **-mus** for 'we', **-tis** for 'you all', **-nt** for 'they'. *manēre* + *-mus* = *manērēmus*; *arāre* + *-nt* = *arārent*.

check.ask: Write the three plural forms on the same infinitive.

teach.title: The passive endings
teach.say: For the passive the same infinitive takes the passive person endings you already use elsewhere: **-r, -ris, -tur, -mur, -minī, -ntur**. *parāre* + *-tur* = *parārētur*, 'was being prepared'; *pāscere* + *-ntur* = *pāscerentur*, 'were being fed'. Once again the infinitive is left whole in front of them.

check.ask: Write the passive 'he was being …' and 'they were being …' forms.

teach.title: The irregular verbs go the same way
teach.say: The verbs that break every other rule keep this one, because it is built on the infinitive and they all have an infinitive: *esse* gives *esset*, *posse* gives *posset*, *velle* gives *vellet*, *īre* gives *īret*, *ferre* gives *ferret*, *fierī* gives *fieret*. If you know the infinitive, you already know the form.

check.ask: posse is the infinitive: write the 'he could' form.

teach.title: Not the present subjunctive, not the infinitive
teach.say: *vidēret* keeps the whole infinitive *vidēre* and adds **-t**; *videat* is built on the short stem *vide-* (the verb minus its ending) with the **-a-** of the present subjunctive: if you can still see the infinitive, it is the past-time form. The **-t** also tells *vidēret* apart from bare *vidēre*: a verb with its own subject, not a 'to' form.
